profile.name: Yangju byeolsandae nori
profile.tagline: Korea's premier designated traditional mask drama born from official defiance.
profile.insight: In Yangju, government officials forged their own mask drama after traveling actors from Hanyang repeatedly broke their performance promises in 19th-century Korea.
profile.profile: Yangju byeolsandae nori is a traditional Korean mask drama that originated in Yangju province when local officials took to producing their own shows after hired entertainers failed to arrive. Performed from evening until dawn in locations like Sagikgol north of Mount Bulgok, the tradition combines rhythmic dancing, miming, and prose dialogue. Accompanied by traditional instruments such as the piri, jeotdae, and janggu, it preserves a complex cast of characters across twenty-two distinct masks.
profile.profile_long:
Yangju byeolsandae nori is Korea's traditional mask drama, registered as an Important Intangible Cultural Properties of Korea. The tradition traces its roots back to sandae gabhee, a welcoming ceremony for Chinese diplomats, and spread mainly from Seoul and Gyeonggi Province across various regions before settling into its distinctive local identity. According to historical accounts from the Korean official culture information service, Yangju byeolsandae nori was started by government officials working in Yangju province. In Yangju, a group of entertainers called Ttakttakyipae from Hanyang came to perform every April and May but they frequently broke their promise and failed to put on a show. Driven by this frustration, the officials in Yangju started to make their own mask drama and hold performances, with Lee Eul-chuk serving as the main organiser and the first producer of mask dramas in the area. At the time, Yangju was both a big town and transport hub, as well as a city populated by many officials, making it an ideal environment for this unique theatrical form.

The performances typically took place in April, May, July, and August, as well as occasionally during ceremonies praying for rain. Before the mask drama started, a ritual ceremony took place praying for a good performance, complete with traditional foods served to honor the occasion. These offerings included jora, tteok, and fruits organized in three colors, alongside the head of a beef and the leg of a pork. Wealthy residents and local merchants funded the costs of the show, while the performers themselves remained unpaid. The staging ground was Sagikgol, located to the north of Mount Bulgok, where a shaman house stood and the props needed for the show were stored. There were no rigid rules regarding the exact duration of performances; they usually started in the evening and continued all the way until dawn the following day, though they were occasionally shortened to three or four hours.

The performance itself is structured around dancing, miming, and drama featuring actors with set prose lines, setting it apart from traditions like Bongsan Talchum whose lines are typically in verse. The movement style is broadly divided into geodeureumsik and kkaekkisik. Musically, the performance relies on traditional Korean instruments, specifically two piri flutes, one jeotdae, one haegeum, one janggu drum, and one buk drum, with a kkwaenggari gong added when needed. Sometimes, players performed with only a piri and janggu, moving to the traditional rhythms of taryong or gutgurigok. While the overarching production involves thirty-two characters, masks are frequently repurposed, meaning only twenty-two physical masks are utilized during any given performance. These roles span a rich spectrum of traditional archetypes, including Sangjwa, lotus flowers, nunkkeumjjeokyi, waejangnyeo, aesadang, somu, veteran figures, monkeys, haesanmo, the podo Director, and miyal grandma.

sections.origins_and_history: Yangju byeolsandae nori was started by government officials working in Yangju province after a group of entertainers called Ttakttakyipae from Hanyang frequently broke their promise to perform. Lee Eul-chuk was the main organiser and first to produce mask dramas in Yangju, leveraging the town's status as a transport hub and administrative center. It traces lineage back to sandae gabhee, a welcoming ceremony for Chinese diplomats, and previously spread to regions like Aeohgae, Manrijae, Gameundol, Nokbeon, Sajikgol, Gupabal, Nodes, Toegyewon, and Uijeongbu.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance is organized primarily around dancing, miming, and drama with actors executing set lines in prose. The dance style is divided into geodeureumsik and kkaekkisik. Some character roles rely entirely on dancing and gestures without spoken words, while others combine dialogue with movement.
sections.music_and_instruments: The main instruments used in the performance are two piri flutes, one jeotdae, one haegeum, one janggu drum, and one buk drum. A kkwaenggari gong is added when needed, and performances occasionally rely solely on the piri and janggu. Musicians utilize the traditional rhythms of taryong or gutgurigok.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances took place at Sagikgol, north of Mount Bulgok, near a shaman house where props were stored. The production features thirty-two traditional characters, but because some masks are utilized in multiple roles, only twenty-two masks are worn during the performance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed primarily in April, May, July, and August, as well as during rain-praying ceremonies. It begins with a ritual ceremony praying for a good performance where traditional foods like jora, tteok, colored fruits, a beef head, and a pork leg are served. Costs were traditionally covered by rich locals and merchants, while performers were unpaid.
sections.notable_figures: Lee Eul-chuk is recorded as the main organiser of the show and the first to produce mask dramas in Yangju.
sections.regional_variants: The tradition spread mainly from Seoul and Gyeonggi Province to Aeohgae, Manrijae, Gameundol, Nokbeon, Sajikgol, Gupabal, Nodes, Toegyewon and Uijeongbu, though it is no longer performed in these external regions.
sections.lineage: Originated from sandae gabhee, a welcoming ceremony for Chinese diplomats, and is also called sandi nori, sanji nori, or sandu nori.

music_profile.sound_description: Played with traditional Korean instruments including two piri flutes, a jeotdae, a haegeum, a janggu drum, and a buk drum, occasionally supplemented by a kkwaenggari gong and driven by taryong or gutgurigok rhythms.
